meta.title: Hardened Financial Domain: Typed Overdraft Exception + Mandatory Entry Direction
meta.hypothesis: Both files coordinate a domain-model hardening: Account.withdraw replaces a silent 0-sentinel with a typed InsufficientFundsError exception, and Ledger.record gains a mandatory EntryKind discriminant — together eliminating two implicit runtime contracts that the TypeScript type system previously could not enforce or express.
meta.summary: Two coordinated breaking changes: (1) Account.withdraw now throws InsufficientFundsError instead of returning 0 on overdraft — callers that pattern-match on the 0 return silently stop detecting overdrafts and instead receive an uncaught exception; (2) Ledger.record gains a mandatory second argument `kind: EntryKind` tagging every entry as 'credit' or 'debit' — all existing direct callers and any code constructing Entry literals break at TypeScript compile-time or silently corrupt entries at JS runtime. The net effect: the financial domain model shifts from permissive and untyped to strict and self-describing, at the cost of a non-backward-compatible API surface across both modules.

tldr.before: Account.withdraw silently returned 0 on overdraft, and ledger.record received no transaction-type label.
tldr.now: Account.withdraw throws a typed InsufficientFundsError on overdraft, and both deposit and withdraw pass 'credit'/'debit' labels to ledger.record.
tldr.behaviorChanged: Yes — callers that checked for a 0 return to detect overdraft now receive an uncaught exception instead, making this a breaking API change.

beacons.note: New InsufficientFundsError class: extends Error, sets this.name for reliable instanceof checks and includes a human-readable message with both requested and available amounts.
Core behavioral pivot in withdraw: balance is cached into 'available' once (avoiding a second ledger call in the error path), and overdraft now throws instead of returning the sentinel 0.

tldr.before: record() accepted only an amount and stored entries with no movement direction on Entry.
tldr.now: record() requires a second mandatory kind: EntryKind argument ('credit'|'debit') that is persisted on every Entry object.
tldr.behaviorChanged: All existing callers of record() and any code constructing Entry literals will break at compile-time (TypeScript) or runtime (JS) because the new required parameter and field are absent.

beacons.note: New EntryKind union type — the semantic anchor of the whole change; constrains the set of valid movement directions to exactly 'credit' or 'debit'.
Entry interface gains a required `kind: EntryKind` field; any existing object literal `{ amount }` is now a type error.
record() signature adds `kind` as a required second parameter and spreads it into the push; the single-expression body means cognitive complexity stays at 0 (estimated).

contracts.postconditionDelta: Introduces a closed union; callers now have a named type to reference instead of raw strings.

contracts.afterSig: interface Entry { amount: number; kind: EntryKind }
contracts.preconditionDelta: Precondition strengthened: every Entry value must now carry a non-optional `kind` field — existing object literals `{ amount }` no longer satisfy the interface.
Precondition strengthened: callers must now supply a second required argument `kind`; any call site omitting it is a compile-time (TS) or silent-undefined (JS) error.
contracts.postconditionDelta: Postcondition strengthened: the pushed Entry is guaranteed to carry `kind`; downstream readers of entries.kind no longer need a missing-field guard.

contracts.afterSig: class InsufficientFundsError extends Error { constructor(requested: number, available: number) }
contracts.postconditionDelta: New export; adds no constraint on existing callers.
Internal only: ledger.record now receives a second argument 'credit'; public observable behavior (void return, balance increases) is unchanged.

contracts.beforeSig: withdraw(amount: number): number  // returns 0 on overdraft
contracts.afterSig: withdraw(amount: number): number  // throws InsufficientFundsError on overdraft
contracts.preconditionDelta: Precondition strengthened: callers must now either ensure amount ≤ balance or catch InsufficientFundsError; previously any amount was safe to call.
contracts.postconditionDelta: Postcondition changed: the return-0 sentinel is gone; overdraft now throws, so the guarantee 'always returns a number' no longer holds.

rippleTargets: callers of Account.withdraw that check result === 0 for overdraft detection
mocks/stubs of Account.withdraw that return 0 to simulate overdraft
direct callers of Ledger.record(amount) without the new kind argument
reporting/audit/reconciliation layers that read or serialize Entry objects

dataflow.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant A as Account
    participant L as Ledger

    Note over C,L: BEFORE — overdraft
    C->>A: withdraw(500), balance=100
    A-->>C: return 0

    Note over C,L: BEFORE — deposit
    C->>A: deposit(200)
    A->>L: record(200)
    Note over L: stores Entry amount=200

    Note over C,L: AFTER — overdraft
    C->>A: withdraw(500), balance=100
    A-->>C: throws InsufficientFundsError

    Note over C,L: AFTER — deposit
    C->>A: deposit(200)
    A->>L: record(200, credit)
    Note over L: stores Entry amount=200 kind=credit

    Note over C,L: AFTER — successful withdraw
    C->>A: withdraw(50), balance=100
    A->>L: record(50, debit)
    Note over L: stores Entry amount=50 kind=debit

narrative.before: Caller invokes Account.withdraw or deposit; Account delegates to Ledger.record(amount) — a single positional argument with no directional tag. On overdraft, withdraw returns 0 in-band and the data pipeline reaches Ledger with no entry recorded. Entries stored in Ledger carry only { amount }, leaving direction implicit and unrecoverable from the record alone.
narrative.after: On overdraft, data flow terminates at Account.withdraw with an exception — no Ledger entry is created, and execution unwinds rather than continuing. On success, withdraw and deposit both pass a 'debit' or 'credit' label as a second argument; Ledger persists Entry { amount, kind }, making movement direction an explicit, mandatory field. Any downstream consumer of Entry objects now receives a richer, directionally-aware record.

detected.name: Sentinel / Error-Code Return
detected.note: withdraw returned 0 as an in-band overdraft signal — a convention invisible to the type system, indistinguishable from a legitimate zero-amount call, and trivially ignored by callers who forget to check.

detected.name: Anemic Entry (no directional semantics)
detected.note: Entry { amount: number } stored a bare number with no information about whether the movement was a credit or debit. Direction was either inferred from context or permanently lost, making reconciliation and auditing fragile.

detected.name: Typed Domain Exception
detected.note: InsufficientFundsError extends Error { constructor(requested, available) } replaces the 0-sentinel with a self-describing exception that carries structured domain context and cannot be silently swallowed by a caller that doesn't explicitly handle it.

detected.name: Discriminated / Sealed Union for Entry Direction
detected.note: export type EntryKind = 'credit' | 'debit' is a closed union that makes the ledger structurally aware of movement direction. TypeScript can now exhaustively check switches over EntryKind, and the type cannot be widened without a deliberate, breaking change.

detected.name: Rich Domain Model (DDD enrichment)
detected.note: Both changes move toward a richer domain model: Account enforces its own overdraft invariant (not delegating that concern to callers), and Entry carries its own directional semantics (not relying on call-site context). This is a DDD pattern — domain objects take responsibility for their own rules and vocabulary.

adr.title: Signal overdraft via typed exception rather than sentinel 0 return
adr.context: Account.withdraw previously returned 0 when balance was insufficient. Callers had to know that 0 meant overdraft — a convention invisible to TypeScript, easily missed in new caller code, and semantically ambiguous (0 is also a valid no-op withdrawal amount in some edge cases).
adr.decision: Throw InsufficientFundsError(requested, available) on overdraft. The error carries structured context and cannot be silently ignored by a caller that doesn't handle exceptions — the failure is self-announcing.
consequences: All callers of Account.withdraw must be audited and updated with try/catch or explicit re-throw
InsufficientFundsError is now part of the public API — must be exported, documented, and kept stable under semver
Any mock or stub of Account that returns 0 to simulate overdraft must be rewritten to throw
If Account is polymorphic (implements IAccount), the exception spec must propagate to the interface definition

options.name: Typed exception (chosen)
pros: Self-documenting: error type conveys domain intent by name
Carries structured data (requested and available amounts) for UI/logging
Cannot be silently ignored — propagates visibly if uncaught
cons: Breaking change: all existing callers must add try/catch or re-throw
Exception-based control flow is contested in JS/TS codebases
Callers must distinguish expected (overdraft) from unexpected (logic error) exceptions
options.bestWhen: Overdraft is truly exceptional — callers should treat it as an interruption to normal flow, not a routine branch

options.name: Result / Either type
pros: Forces callers to handle both success and failure paths structurally
No hidden control flow — failure is a value, not an exception
cons: No native TS/JS support — requires a library or hand-rolled type
More verbose at call sites (must destructure ok/error)
Does not compose naturally with async/await error propagation
options.bestWhen: Overdraft is a common, expected outcome that callers frequently branch on without exception plumbing

behavioral.conditionalEquivalence: Unchanged except when a withdrawal would overdraft the account (now throws InsufficientFundsError instead of returning 0) or when any code calls Ledger.record() or constructs an Entry without the new required kind argument (now a compile error in TypeScript or a silent kind: undefined corruption in plain JS).

traceCards.input: account.withdraw(500) on an Account with balance = 100
traceCards.beforeOutput: Returns numeric 0; caller's execution continues normally past the call site
traceCards.afterOutput: Throws InsufficientFundsError({ requested: 500, available: 100 }); call stack unwinds to the nearest try/catch or crashes if unhandled

divergentState.name: caller execution flow
divergentState.before: continues past withdraw() — the 0 return value is received and any downstream if (result === 0) check fires as expected
divergentState.after: interrupted at withdraw() — execution jumps to the exception handler, bypassing all code between the call site and the catch block

divergentState.name: overdraft detection
divergentState.before: caller must explicitly check if (result === 0) using domain knowledge that 0 signals overdraft
divergentState.after: exception is self-announcing; no explicit check needed, but callers that relied on the 0-check are now silently broken

traceCards.gwt: Given an Account with balance 100, When withdraw(500) is called, Then before: caller receives 0 and execution silently continues; after: InsufficientFundsError is thrown and the call stack unwinds

traceCards.beforeOutput: ledger.record(200) called; Entry { amount: 200 } stored with no directional field
traceCards.afterOutput: ledger.record(200, 'credit') called; Entry { amount: 200, kind: 'credit' } stored with explicit direction

divergentState.name: Entry shape in Ledger
divergentState.before: { amount: 200 } — direction is absent and unrecoverable from the stored record
divergentState.after: { amount: 200, kind: 'credit' } — direction is explicit and queryable downstream

traceCards.gwt: Given a deposit of 200, When the ledger records it, Then the stored Entry now carries kind: 'credit' alongside the amount, making movement direction an explicit first-class field

traceCards.input: ledger.record(100) called directly by a legacy caller without a kind argument
traceCards.beforeOutput: Entry { amount: 100 } stored successfully; no compiler error
traceCards.afterOutput: TypeScript: compile error 'Expected 2 arguments, but got 1'; plain JavaScript runtime: Entry { amount: 100, kind: undefined } stored silently with a corrupted kind field

divergentState.name: kind field on stored Entry
divergentState.before: absent — the interface did not define it; omitting it was correct
divergentState.after: undefined at JS runtime (silent data corruption) or a compile error under TypeScript (caught early)

divergentState.name: compilation
divergentState.after: TypeScript rejects the call; plain JS silently stores a malformed entry

traceCards.gwt: Given a direct caller of ledger.record(amount) without a kind argument, When compiled under TypeScript or executed as plain JS, Then TypeScript rejects at compile time; plain JS stores kind: undefined on the Entry without error

behavioral.workedExample: Before: `const result = account.withdraw(500); if (result === 0) { alert('overdraft!'); }` — the if-branch fires and the alert is shown. After: `account.withdraw(500)` throws InsufficientFundsError before the if-check is ever reached — the alert never fires, and if there is no enclosing try/catch, the process crashes instead. The silent regression is the dangerous part: the code looks the same but the overdraft is no longer caught.

callers: callers checking result === 0 for overdraft detection
mocks/stubs that return 0 to simulate overdraft in tests
any module calling record(amount) without the new kind argument
reporting, audit, or reconciliation layers that read or serialize Entry objects

behavioral.eli5: Think of the overdraft check like a fire alarm. Before, if you tried to take out more money than you had, the ATM quietly handed you $0 and hoped you'd notice something was wrong. Now it sets off the fire alarm the moment you try — you cannot miss it, but it also means everyone nearby has to deal with the alarm going off. Users now get a proper 'not enough funds' error instead of mystery $0 transactions that slip through unnoticed.
behavioral.junior: withdraw() used to return 0 as a sentinel for overdraft — callers had to explicitly check `if (result === 0)` to detect failure. Now it throws InsufficientFundsError, which propagates up the call stack to the nearest try/catch. Any existing caller that was checking for 0 is now broken in a subtle way: the exception fires and unwinds past their check before it ever runs, so overdraft now looks like a crash rather than a handled branch.
behavioral.senior: The error-signaling channel changed from in-band return value (0 as overdraft code) to out-of-band exception. Call sites that pattern-match `result === 0` don't fail loudly — the exception unwinds past them, so overdraft now produces crashes or unhandled-rejection warnings rather than the expected conditional branch. The Ledger.record change is separately dangerous in JS: callers without the new kind argument store `kind: undefined` silently — a runtime data corruption that TypeScript catches at compile time but that plain-JS runtimes let through without a word.
behavioral.architect: Two invariant shifts: (1) withdraw changes its error-channel from return-value domain code to exception, invalidating the substitution assumption for any decorator, adapter, or proxy wrapping withdraw that currently intercepts 0-returns — those wrappers now pass the exception through unhandled; (2) Ledger.record enforces double-entry direction at the persistence boundary via EntryKind, making the schema structurally aware of credit/debit semantics rather than treating all entries as unsigned scalars. The ripple extends to any reporting, audit, or reconciliation layer that reads Entry objects — they gain a mandatory field and must handle the migration gap for any pre-change persisted entries that lack kind.

dependency.eli5: Account and Ledger already talked to each other. Now when Account tells Ledger to write down a transaction, it also says whether money came in or went out — like writing 'deposit' or 'withdrawal' next to every amount in the ledger book, instead of just the number.
dependency.junior: The account.ts → ledger.ts dependency edge already existed. What changed is the payload on that edge: Account now passes 'credit' or 'debit' as a second argument to Ledger.record(). The import statement is unchanged; the interface contract on the edge tightened from a single-argument to a two-argument call.
dependency.senior: The dependency direction is unchanged (Account → Ledger), but the call signature on the edge went from record(amount) to record(amount, kind), making the edge contract stricter. This is not isolated to Account: any other module that also depends on Ledger.record directly inherits this breakage. The fan-out of the breaking change scales with the number of Ledger consumers, not just the number of Account callers.
dependency.architect: Ledger.record's required kind parameter is a fan-out breaking change propagated through the Ledger interface. If Ledger is injected via an interface or abstract class (ILedger), the interface definition must be updated first, all implementations must conform before any call sites migrate, and any DI container registration that binds ILedger must be re-validated. This is an ordered migration — it cannot be parallelized safely across all consumers without an intermediate optional-kind shim.

contract.eli5: The rules for using these two functions officially changed. You must now say 'credit' or 'debit' when recording any money movement, and the bank will no longer silently pretend an overdraft succeeded — it will tell you exactly how much you asked for and how much was actually available.
contract.junior: withdraw has a new postcondition: it throws InsufficientFundsError when amount > balance. record has a new precondition: kind must be provided as 'credit' or 'debit'. These are formal contract changes, not implementation details — callers are now obligated by the type system and runtime behavior to handle them.
contract.senior: The withdrawal guard changed from soft (return 0 if violated) to hard (throw if violated). The Entry postcondition changed from { amount } to { amount, kind } — any schema validation, serialization, or equality check that previously accepted Entry must be updated to require kind. The implicit contract that 'all Entry values have only an amount field' is now broken at the interface level, not just at the implementation level.
contract.architect: InsufficientFundsError is now part of the exception specification (the implicit 'throws' contract) of Account.withdraw. If Account is polymorphic, the exception spec must propagate to IAccount and all implementors. EntryKind as a closed string union is a future change-risk: adding 'transfer' or 'fee' later widens the union and is another breaking change for any exhaustive switch/match over EntryKind — a design constraint the team should document now to avoid surprise.

dataflow.eli5: Every time money moves now, the record it leaves behind has a direction arrow stamped right on it — it says 'in' (credit) or 'out' (debit). Before, you just got the number and had to guess which direction the money was moving from context somewhere else in the code.
dataflow.junior: Before: deposit(amount) → record(amount) → Entry { amount }. After: deposit(amount) → record(amount, 'credit') → Entry { amount, kind: 'credit' }. The kind value flows from Account through Ledger into the stored Entry. On the overdraft path, data flow now terminates at Account.withdraw with an exception — no ledger entry is created at all.
dataflow.senior: The Entry data shape changed: { amount } → { amount, kind }. Any downstream consumer of Entry objects (reports, reconciliation exports, analytics) now receives an extra mandatory field and must handle it. On failed withdrawals, the data pipeline now terminates at Account — previously a 0-amount or 0-return record may have existed depending on implementation; now no Ledger trace is produced on overdraft, which is a data-completeness gap if audit logging of failed attempts was an implicit requirement.
dataflow.architect: The EntryKind addition to Entry is a one-way schema migration concern: existing persisted entries lack the kind field. If Entry is persisted to a database or event store, a migration strategy is required — either a backfill (all historical entries tagged as 'unknown' or a legacy sentinel), a nullable column with application-layer fallback, or an event-sourcing replay. The exception path in withdraw also creates an audit gap: failed overdraft attempts no longer produce a ledger trace. If regulatory compliance requires recording all attempted withdrawals, the caller must now explicitly catch InsufficientFundsError and emit a separate audit event — a responsibility that previously happened implicitly (via the 0-return path) if the old code called record before checking the balance.
